title: Shadow theatre on my dorm wall
introduction: This week’s assignment was to create a piece suitable for projection or digital display. I chose the running stick figure from my Week 2 and Week 5 pieces, cropped it into a flat card, and held it in front of a photograph of a real wall in my room. A virtual handheld lamp illuminated the card and projected its shadow onto the wall. Everything was computer-generated: there was no physical card, no real lamp, and certainly no p5. Each frame was drawn individually using Python and stitched together using ffmpeg.
related_work: Shadow puppetry is the oldest form of projection: all it requires is light, an object and a wall. In this week’s lecture, Sean Cubitt pointed out that projection is a practice of light, rather than the operation of a machine. Two of these perspectives are directly incorporated into this work. He described the Lascaux cave paintings as seen ‘by a flickering torch, not unlike the flicker of cinema’; he also revisited Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, where the prisoners see only the shadows cast by a fire they cannot see; without the fire, there would be no shadows at all. Ryan highlighted the distinction between projection and illumination at the outset of his lecture: a screen emits light of its own, whereas a projected image is an image cast onto a surface by borrowed light.
method: This lamp is a point light source. When it is far from the card, the shadow it casts is small and sharp; when it is closer and positioned lower, the shadow extends to the top of the wall, with its edges gradually softening to form a penumbra. The magnification ratio depends solely on two distances, the distance from the lamp to the wall divided by the distance from the lamp to the card, so the shape of the projection remains constant, with only the position of the lamp changing. As it is a handheld lamp, it trembles slightly. After the lecture, I added two further elements. Now, the lamp takes five seconds to light up, transitioning from complete darkness to dim light and then to full brightness, whilst flickering like a torch: three sets of sine waves at different speeds are superimposed, ensuring that the flickering pattern is never repeated. The AI wrote the Python script and created the template for the lamp. I conceived the piece, set the lamp’s movement trajectory and timing parameters, and repeatedly adjusted the various values (the time required for the fade-in, the intensity of the flickering, and the moment it switches off) until I was satisfied with the lighting effects.
results_discussion: The figure in the projection cannot determine its own size. Whoever holds the light determines the size, clarity and duration of the silhouette’s visibility. This is the power dynamic underlying every projection: the person operating the projector determines what the audience sees. The shift in sensation brought about by the flickering effect exceeded my expectations. Steady light evokes an office setting; flickering light, on the other hand, brings to mind a flame, and the silhouette thus transforms from an object on display into an object of gaze.
conclusion_future_work: This work begins in darkness and ends in darkness. When the lights go out, everything returns to nothingness; this is precisely the fundamental distinction between projection- based works and screen-based works. The same stick figure has now spanned three weeks: it appeared in Week 2, was given a voice in Week 5, and transformed into a shadow in Week 7. Each time, the figure itself remains unchanged; it is the layers surrounding it that change.
